messages.content: I want to develop RLHF that preserves conflicting minority preferences under policy-induced distribution shifts, without observing annotator group identities. The goals are to improve the worst-group preference win rate by at least 5 percentage points versus pooled RLHF with matching feedback budgets, and to establish identifiability conditions that separate persistent preference disagreement from annotation noise under distribution shift. Can you help me articulate what those goals require?

There are two connected goals. The performance goal is comparative: the proposed RLHF approach should achieve a worst-group preference win rate at least 5 percentage points higher than pooled RLHF, with the feedback budgets matched. The inference goal is to establish conditions under which the available observations can distinguish enduring differences in preferences from variability caused by annotation noise, even as the policy changes what is encountered and annotated. The absence of observed annotator group identities matters to both goals: the approach cannot rely on those identities as an input, and any claim about a worst group needs a defensible interpretation and evaluation.
What does it mean to preserve conflicting minority preferences, rather than just improve an average preference score?

The word “conflicting” matters because the preferences of a minority may genuinely favor a different response from the one favored by others. Preserving them means not treating that disagreement as something that must disappear into a single pooled preference. An average score could improve while outcomes for the least well-served preference group do not. That is why the stated performance target concerns the worst-group preference win rate, not merely a pooled or average win rate.
Does “minority” imply that I already know which annotators belong to it?

No. The goal explicitly says annotator group identities are not observed. “Minority preferences” describes the kind of disagreement the RLHF approach is meant to preserve; it does not grant access to group labels during feedback collection or learning. Identifying what can be inferred without those labels is part of the difficulty, rather than a detail that can be assumed away.
And why is the policy-induced distribution shift part of the goal?

Because an RLHF policy can change the distribution of responses and comparisons on which feedback is obtained. If the observations change as the policy changes, an apparent change in preferences might reflect a change in what people were asked to judge, rather than a change in their underlying preferences. The goal is to preserve conflicting minority preferences under that shifting distribution, not only in a setting where the feedback distribution stays fixed.
Could that shift also make a persistent disagreement look like annotation noise?

Potentially. If different kinds of comparisons become more or less common, variability in the observed annotations may have several explanations. Some of it could reflect consistent disagreement between people with different preferences; some could reflect noise in how a preference is expressed. The identifiability goal asks when those explanations can be separated from the observations, rather than assuming that every conflicting annotation is noise or that every conflict reveals a persistent preference difference.
So is the task to eliminate annotation noise?

Not as stated. The task is to establish identifiability conditions separating persistent preference disagreement from annotation noise under distribution shift. That is a question about when the two can be told apart. Better handling of noise may be relevant to an eventual method, but the specified goal does not say that noise can be eliminated or that all disagreement should be resolved into a single preference.
What exactly is the numerical target?

It is an improvement of at least 5 percentage points in worst-group preference win rate relative to pooled RLHF, with matching feedback budgets. “Percentage points” denotes an absolute difference in win-rate percentages: for a purely hypothetical illustration, a worst-group win rate of 65% compared with 60% for pooled RLHF would be a 5-percentage-point improvement. Those illustrative numbers are not reported results or specified baselines.
Why specify matching feedback budgets?

It keeps the comparison focused on what the RLHF approach accomplishes with the same amount of feedback available to pooled RLHF. Otherwise, an apparent advantage could simply reflect receiving more feedback. The requirement specifies matched feedback budgets; it does not, by itself, settle every other possible aspect of a comparison.
Is pooled RLHF the thing the worst group is compared against, or is the worst group compared with the average group?

Pooled RLHF is the stated method baseline. The specified improvement is in worst-group preference win rate versus pooled RLHF, under matching feedback budgets. It is not a requirement to beat an average group by 5 percentage points. Care is needed to compare the same kind of worst-group quantity on both sides, rather than silently switching from a worst-group measure to an average one.
If annotator group identities are unobserved, is it contradictory to talk about a worst-group win rate?

It creates a challenge, but not necessarily a contradiction. The method cannot assume observed annotator group identities. At the same time, a worst-group performance claim requires a defensible account of what the relevant groups are and how their preference win rates can be assessed. The goal does not supply an evaluation procedure, so it would be premature to claim that this has already been resolved or to assume access to group labels as part of the learning input.
Could I just interpret every minority-looking annotation as evidence of a separate group?

That would not, on its own, establish persistent preference disagreement. A minority-looking annotation could arise from a stable conflicting preference, annotation noise, or the mix of comparisons observed under the changing policy. The identifiability requirement exists precisely because these explanations should not be conflated. A claim about a persistent preference difference needs conditions under which that explanation can be distinguished from noise.
What does “identifiability conditions” mean here, without pretending we already know them?

It means stating the assumptions or observational circumstances under which persistent preference disagreement and annotation noise would have distinguishable implications for the feedback that can be observed, despite distribution shift. It also means recognizing cases where they would be observationally indistinguishable. The current goal calls for establishing those conditions; it does not provide them or assert that identification is always possible.
Can you give me a conceptual picture of when they might be indistinguishable?

Imagine observing inconsistent judgments on comparisons, but having no information that connects those judgments to stable differences in preference. One explanation could be that different people consistently favor different outcomes; another could be that people share a preference but sometimes provide noisy annotations. If those explanations imply the same observable feedback in the setting under consideration, the data alone cannot choose between them. A policy-induced change in which comparisons are observed adds another possible source of ambiguity. That is a conceptual illustration, not a claim about a particular dataset.
Would seeing the same disagreement more than once settle it?

Repetition may be informative, but repetition alone does not automatically settle the distinction. Its value depends on what is repeated, what can be linked across observations, and what assumptions are made about noise and the shifting distribution. The identifiability goal is to make such requirements explicit, rather than treating recurring disagreement as sufficient proof of distinct, persistent preferences.
I also do not want “under distribution shift” to get dropped from the identifiability part.

It should remain explicit in both parts of the goal. The RLHF approach is meant to preserve conflicting minority preferences under policy-induced distribution shifts. Separately, the identifiability conditions must address how persistent preference disagreement can be separated from annotation noise under distribution shift. A distinction that works only when the observation distribution is fixed would not, without further justification, establish the stated identifiability goal.
Is this asking for a guaranteed improvement in every possible setting?

The node sets a target—at least a 5-percentage-point improvement in worst-group preference win rate versus pooled RLHF with matching feedback budgets—but it does not assert a universal guarantee across every possible setting. The identifiability component likewise calls for conditions, which implies being clear about when the distinction can be made and when the available observations do not support it. Neither goal is an accomplished result here.
How should I avoid accidentally turning the minority-preference goal into a claim that all preferences can be satisfied at once?

Keep the word “conflicting” in view. If preferences conflict, an outcome preferred by one set of people may not be preferred by another. Preserving minority preferences does not mean asserting that every comparison has a universally preferred answer. It means developing RLHF with attention to those persistent conflicts and evaluating the stated worst-group win-rate target, rather than assuming a pooled preference captures everyone equally well.
What is the concise version I could use to check whether a description remains faithful to the goal?

It should say that the work aims to develop RLHF that preserves conflicting minority preferences under policy-induced distribution shifts without observing annotator group identities. It should retain both requirements: at least a 5-percentage-point improvement in worst-group preference win rate over pooled RLHF at matching feedback budgets, and identifiability conditions for distinguishing persistent preference disagreement from annotation noise under distribution shift. It should present those as goals to achieve, not as results already established.

For the approach, I’m proposing that we cluster pseudonymous annotators using repeated anchor comparisons, then train importance-weighted minimax RLHF targeting worst-cluster preference win rate under policy shifts. Can you unpack that without treating it as an established result?

Yes. The proposal has two connected parts. First, repeated anchor comparisons provide a basis for clustering annotators whose feedback can be associated with pseudonyms, without observing their group identities. Second, importance-weighted minimax RLHF uses those clusters to target the preference win rate of the worst-performing cluster while accounting for policy shifts. This describes a proposed approach, not a demonstrated improvement or a claim that the clusters reveal true group identities.
Why specify pseudonymous annotators rather than just annotators?

Pseudonyms let the proposal refer to feedback associated with an annotator across observations without requiring knowledge of that person’s group identity. That continuity matters to the idea of clustering from repeated comparisons. A pseudonym is not itself a demographic label, a known preference group, or proof that the person belongs to a particular cluster for any reason beyond the feedback used for clustering.
And what work are the repeated anchor comparisons meant to do?

They give the clustering step recurring comparisons against which annotators’ expressed preferences can be related. Conceptually, repeated anchors provide more of a basis for assessing whether patterns of disagreement persist than unrelated, one-off judgments would. The proposal does not specify how many repetitions are needed or establish that the anchors alone distinguish stable preferences from annotation noise.
So the anchors do not magically supply group identities?

Correct. Their proposed role is to help cluster pseudonymous annotators based on comparison feedback. The resulting clusters would be constructed from observed responses, not read from known annotator group labels. Whether a cluster faithfully reflects a persistent preference difference is a question to examine, not an assumption that follows just from calling the comparisons anchors.
I want to be precise about the word “cluster.” Is a cluster necessarily the same as a minority preference group?

No. In this proposal, a cluster is an inferred grouping of pseudonymous annotators. It may be useful for representing differences in expressed preferences, but the proposal does not establish a one-to-one correspondence between clusters and underlying preference groups. In particular, targeting the worst-cluster preference win rate is the method’s stated target; it should not automatically be described as a measured worst-group outcome.
What does the minimax part contribute?

It expresses the intention to train against the weakest cluster-level preference outcome rather than optimize only an aggregate across all feedback. In that sense, the proposed training target is the worst-cluster preference win rate. The term does not, by itself, specify an optimization formula, prove that the worst cluster can always be identified reliably, or guarantee a particular level of improvement.
Could you distinguish that from simply weighting each cluster equally?

They are different ideas. Equal cluster weighting would give clusters the same contribution to an aggregate objective. A minimax target focuses on the cluster with the weakest preference win rate. The proposal specifies the latter target, alongside importance weighting; it does not state that equal cluster weighting is the training rule.
Where does importance weighting enter the picture?

It is the proposed way to make training sensitive to the fact that policy shifts change the distribution of feedback-relevant comparisons. Conceptually, weighting can address how much observations from one policy-induced distribution should count when targeting performance under another. The proposal calls for importance-weighted minimax RLHF but does not specify particular weights, how they would be obtained, or conditions under which they would be reliable.
Would it be accurate to say that importance weighting solves distribution shift?

That would overstate it. Importance weighting is part of the proposed response to policy shifts, not a blanket solution. Whether it adequately accounts for a shift depends on circumstances that are not established here. The faithful phrasing is that the proposed RLHF training is importance-weighted and targets worst-cluster preference win rate under policy shifts.
Why connect the weighting and minimax parts rather than mentioning them separately?

Because they address different aspects of the same proposed training objective. The minimax aspect says whose preference win rate receives attention: the worst-performing inferred cluster. The importance-weighted aspect addresses how feedback is counted in the presence of policy shifts. Keeping both in view avoids describing a worst-cluster objective as though the distribution of observed comparisons could never change.
Could a policy shift affect the clustering too, or only the subsequent RLHF training?

It could matter when interpreting the comparison feedback used for clustering: changes in what gets compared can change what is observable about annotators’ preferences. The proposal explicitly places importance weighting in the minimax RLHF training step under policy shifts; it does not specify a separate shift-correction procedure for clustering. So it is reasonable to note the interpretive issue without claiming that the proposal has already resolved it.
If a small cluster has a low win rate, does minimax training necessarily preserve a genuine minority preference?

Not necessarily. The objective would target the worst cluster as constructed, but a small or poorly supported cluster need not correspond to a genuine, persistent minority preference. Repeated anchor comparisons are proposed as a basis for clustering; they do not automatically validate every cluster. The distinction between a worst inferred cluster and a genuine underlying preference group remains important.
Does this proposal establish when disagreement is persistent rather than annotation noise?

No. Clustering from repeated anchor comparisons could provide evidence relevant to that distinction, but the proposal alone does not state identifiability conditions or prove that persistent disagreement can always be separated from annotation noise under distribution shift. It is a candidate approach to organizing feedback and training RLHF, not a completed identifiability result.
Am I committing to a particular clustering algorithm or a particular formula for the importance weights?

Not in this proposal. It specifies the use of repeated anchor comparisons to cluster pseudonymous annotators and importance-weighted minimax RLHF to target worst-cluster preference win rate under policy shifts. It leaves the clustering algorithm, weighting formula, and detailed training procedure unspecified.
Can I say the proposal avoids using annotator group identities while still using information about individual annotators?

Yes, with the distinction made explicit. It uses pseudonymous continuity in annotator feedback for clustering, rather than observed annotator group identities. “No observed group identities” does not mean there can be no way to associate repeated feedback with a pseudonymous annotator; that association is part of the proposed clustering step.
What would be a misleading shorthand for the objective?

Saying “optimize the worst known group” would be misleading, because the proposal clusters pseudonymous annotators rather than starting with known group identities. Saying “optimize the average preference” would also miss the minimax target. The closer shorthand is “target the worst inferred cluster’s preference win rate using importance-weighted minimax RLHF under policy shifts,” while retaining the qualification that clusters are inferred.
I also do not want to imply that importance weighting makes every policy shift harmless.

Then describe it as a proposed component intended to account for policy-induced changes in the feedback distribution, not as a guarantee of shift-invariant performance. The approach still needs to be assessed on whether its weighting and cluster-based objective work under the policy shifts of interest.
Can you put the proposal into one sentence that keeps the ordering of the steps?
Cluster pseudonymous annotators using repeated anchor comparisons, then train an importance-weighted minimax RLHF approach that targets worst-cluster preference win rate under policy shifts.
And the key caution when discussing that sentence?

Treat it as a proposed method: the clusters are inferred from feedback rather than observed group identities, and neither the usefulness of those clusters nor the effectiveness of importance weighting and minimax training has been established by the proposal itself.
Under what shared-anchor repetition and policy-support overlap are latent preference clusters identifiable separately from annotator-specific noise?

That is an identifiability question, not one with a repetition count or overlap threshold already specified. A useful answer would have to state assumptions under which distinct latent preference clusters and annotator-specific noise imply distinguishable patterns in the observed feedback. It would also have to say which shared anchor comparisons recur across pseudonymous annotators and remain observable across the policy shifts being considered. Repetition and overlap can supply information, but neither alone proves that the clusters are identifiable.
What does “shared” add to the anchor requirement?

It means the anchors must connect annotators’ responses to comparisons they have in common. Repeating judgments for each pseudonymous annotator could tell us something about that annotator’s consistency, but if different annotators never judge comparable anchors, it is harder to determine whether their response patterns reflect the same preference or different ones. Shared anchors provide a common reference for asking whether disagreement persists across annotators.
Is one shared response from each annotator enough to separate a cluster from noise?

Not in general. A single response could reflect a stable preference or a noisy annotation. Repetition can make patterns of consistency and disagreement more observable, but there is no specified number of repeats that automatically resolves the distinction. What repetition establishes depends on assumptions about how annotator-specific noise behaves and on whether the anchors actually reveal the preference differences of interest.
When you say repetition, do you mean repeating an anchor for the same pseudonym or showing anchors to several pseudonyms?

Both connections matter conceptually. Repetition for the same pseudonym can bear on whether that person’s expressed preference is stable across observations. Sharing anchors across pseudonyms can bear on whether stable patterns align or conflict between annotators. Neither connection should be silently substituted for the other when stating identifiability conditions.
Suppose the answers to a shared anchor keep differing between pseudonyms. Can I call those latent clusters?

You could investigate whether the differences support latent clusters, but recurring differences alone do not settle it. For example, the interpretation depends on whether the same pseudonyms tend to give stable answers and on what sorts of annotator-specific noise remain possible. If the noise model allows persistent, annotator-specific response tendencies that look just like preferences on the anchors, those tendencies and latent preference clusters may be observationally indistinguishable. An identifiability claim would need to confront that ambiguity rather than label every persistent difference a cluster.
That sounds like a particularly difficult boundary: persistent preference versus persistent annotator-specific noise.

Yes. Mere persistence cannot separate two explanations if both are allowed to persist in the same observable way. The conditions would need to say what is meant by annotator-specific noise, how it differs from the preference variation being sought, and what observable consequences follow from that distinction. Without a restriction of that kind, the same response pattern could be described using either explanation.
Does this mean I must assume annotations are independent?

Not necessarily. An assumption about independence could be one way to make repeated responses informative, but the question does not prescribe that assumption. The important point is to make any proposed assumptions about noise explicit and check whether they really distinguish it from persistent preference disagreement. Calling responses “noise” without specifying what patterns noise can and cannot produce would not establish identifiability.
How informative do the anchor comparisons themselves have to be?

They must provide information relevant to the distinctions being claimed. If two latent preference patterns make the same judgments on every shared anchor that is observable, those anchors cannot separate the patterns, however often they are repeated. Conversely, disagreement on informative shared anchors might help distinguish patterns, subject to the noise assumptions. The question asks for the conditions under which that distinction is possible; it does not already identify a sufficient set of anchors.
What is the role of policy-support overlap in that question?

Policy shifts can change which comparisons are encountered and therefore where preference feedback is observed. Support overlap concerns whether comparisons relevant to distinguishing clusters remain represented across the distributions induced by the policies under consideration. If a relevant kind of comparison is absent under one policy, observations under that policy alone cannot reveal how the latent preferences would differ on it. Overlap matters for relating evidence across shifts, rather than assuming the observations from different policies are directly interchangeable.
Does overlap have to cover every imaginable comparison?

The question does not specify such a universal requirement. The pertinent issue is whether overlap covers the comparisons needed for the particular cluster distinctions and shift-related claims being made. Requiring overlap everywhere would be a much broader statement; having overlap somewhere, but not where competing preference explanations differ, may be insufficient. The identifiability conditions would need to state the relevant scope.
Could extensive anchor repetition compensate for no policy-support overlap?

It cannot create observations of comparisons that the shifted policy never places in support. Repetition may clarify response patterns on observed anchors, but it cannot by itself identify preferences on an unobserved part of the relevant comparison space. The two requirements address different potential gaps: whether feedback is repeated and connected across annotators, and whether the necessary comparisons remain observable across policy shifts.
What if there is some overlap but it is very limited?

Then it matters what the overlap contains. If it connects only comparisons on which the proposed clusters behave alike, it may not distinguish them. If the relevant comparisons are observable but extremely uncommon, there is also a difference between identification in principle and being able to estimate a distinction reliably from a finite amount of feedback. The question does not set a quantitative overlap threshold or feedback amount, so neither conclusion should be asserted without further conditions.
Would importance weighting settle the overlap issue?

Importance weighting cannot supply feedback for a comparison that has no support in the observations being weighted. Where there is overlap, weighting may be relevant to accounting for a policy-induced change in the distribution, but it does not replace the need for informative shared anchors or assumptions that distinguish preferences from annotator-specific noise. Whether weighting is reliable when overlap is limited is a separate question from whether the latent clusters are identifiable at all.
Can a distribution shift make it look as though annotators changed preferences, even if their preferences persisted?

Conceptually, yes: if the mix of comparisons changes, the mix of observed judgments can change without any underlying preference changing. To identify latent clusters separately from noise under that shift, the account must relate observations across policies rather than interpret each change in the aggregate response pattern as a change in preferences. Shared informative comparisons and appropriate support overlap are pertinent to making that relation possible.
Is the issue only whether two clusters differ, or also whether we can tell which pseudonymous annotator belongs to which cluster?

Those are distinct claims. Evidence might support the existence of differing preference patterns without assigning every pseudonymous annotator to a cluster with certainty. Conversely, a procedure can assign cluster labels without establishing that the labels represent identifiable preference differences rather than noise. The identifiability question should be explicit about whether it concerns distinguishable latent patterns, annotator assignments, or both.
Would the literal names of the clusters matter to identifiability?

No. If two inferred clusters can be distinguished only up to exchanging their names, that naming ambiguity is different from being unable to distinguish the preference patterns themselves. The substantive question is whether the patterns and their separation from annotator-specific noise have observable meaning, not whether one is called “cluster one” rather than “cluster two.”
Can you describe a failure case without claiming that it occurs in our setting?

As a general illustration, suppose all observed shared anchors elicit the same response pattern from two hypothesized preference clusters, while comparisons on which they would differ are never observed after a policy shift. Repeating the observed anchors cannot reveal that distinction. Alternatively, if a proposed noise model permits an annotator to respond consistently in exactly the way attributed to a latent preference cluster, the observations may not distinguish those explanations. These are examples of why the required conditions need to be stated, not findings about a particular set of feedback.
And what would a favorable case need, at a conceptual level?

It would need shared anchors that expose relevant differences, enough repeated and connected observations for persistent patterns to be meaningfully assessed, assumptions that give annotator-specific noise different observable implications from latent preferences, and policy-support overlap sufficient to carry the relevant comparisons across shifts. That is a conceptual checklist, not a theorem or a claim that a particular amount of repetition and overlap is sufficient.
I want the question to remain open rather than quietly turning that checklist into an answer.

Then phrase the checklist as what must be examined. The open question is which forms and amounts of shared-anchor repetition, together with which degree of policy-support overlap and which assumptions about annotator-specific noise, permit identification of latent preference clusters. In particular, neither a universal repetition count nor a sufficient overlap condition has been established here.

Here is a hypothesis for the identifiability question: three repeated shared anchors, independent symmetric noise below 50%, distinct cluster signatures, and positive policy overlap identify persistent disagreement. Can we unpack exactly what that claims?

It proposes a joint set of conditions under which persistent preference disagreement can be identified separately from annotator-specific noise despite policy shifts. The conditions are three repeated shared anchors, independent symmetric noise below 50%, distinct cluster signatures, and positive policy overlap. It is a hypothesis of sufficiency, not an established identifiability result or a statement that any one condition works on its own.
Does “three repeated shared anchors” mean three repetitions of one comparison?

The wording specifies three shared anchors that are repeated. It should not be silently changed to one anchor repeated three times, or to exactly three observations per anchor. The proposed role of repetition is to make response patterns on common comparisons observable again, while sharing gives different pseudonymous annotators a common basis for comparison. The hypothesis does not specify a repetition schedule beyond that wording.
Why would repeating shared anchors help distinguish persistent disagreement from noise?

The intuition is that a persistent preference difference should produce a recurring pattern across the shared anchors, whereas independent noise should not systematically create the same pattern in repeated observations. That intuition depends on the other stated conditions, especially what independence and symmetry mean for the noise and whether cluster signatures really differ. It motivates the hypothesis; it is not yet a proof that three repeated shared anchors suffice.
What work is the “independent symmetric noise below 50%” assumption doing?

It constrains the noise explanation. Symmetry says, at a conceptual level, that annotation errors do not systematically favor one of the competing judgments; independence says they do not persist together in a way that simply mimics a stable preference pattern. The below-50% condition says the noise rate is strictly less than 50%, not equal to it. Together, those properties are intended to leave a distinguishable signal of persistent disagreement in repeated feedback. A precise identifiability argument would still need to define the noise process and establish that the stated assumptions have the intended implications.
Should I say the noise rate is at most 50%?
No. “Below 50%” is strict. “At most 50%” would include 50%, which changes the stated condition. Keeping the threshold exact matters when describing the hypothesis.
Does independent noise mean different annotators can never disagree?

No. Independence concerns the noise, not a prohibition on disagreement. The hypothesis is specifically about identifying persistent disagreement, so it allows distinct preference patterns. It proposes that the noise component behaves independently and symmetrically, with a rate below 50%, rather than assuming every difference between annotators must be a noisy error.
Can I take “independent” to mean independent across every annotator, comparison, and policy?

The hypothesis uses the word “independent” but does not spell out all the indices over which independence is assumed. A formal version would need to specify that scope. It would be an additional commitment to declare, without qualification, that independence holds across every annotator, comparison, and policy.
What are distinct cluster signatures contributing?

They provide something for the shared anchors to distinguish. If putative clusters have indistinguishable patterns on the relevant observable comparisons, repetition cannot tell those patterns apart. The hypothesis therefore requires distinct cluster signatures alongside repeated shared anchors and its noise assumption. It does not specify a particular distance between signatures or claim that every annotator’s cluster assignment becomes certain.
Is a distinct signature just a different label assigned by the clustering procedure?

No. Merely assigning different labels would not establish an observable preference distinction. “Distinct cluster signatures” refers to differing preference patterns associated with the proposed clusters. The hypothesis is about whether those differences can be identified as persistent disagreement, not whether a clustering procedure can produce multiple names for groups of responses.
How does positive policy overlap enter the hypothesis?

It is the condition connecting relevant observations across policy-induced distribution shifts. If comparisons needed to recognize the distinct signatures have no support where they are needed, feedback cannot reveal those distinctions there. Positive policy overlap is proposed to prevent that kind of complete observational gap. The hypothesis says “positive”; it does not give a numerical minimum for the amount of overlap.
So does positive overlap mean the comparison distributions have to be identical before and after a policy shift?

No. Overlap is compatible with a shift: distributions can change while still sharing support. The proposed condition is positive policy overlap, not an unchanged comparison distribution. The question is whether the overlap connects the observations relevant to identifying the distinct preference signatures.
Would a tiny positive overlap satisfy the wording?

The wording does not set a lower bound beyond positivity. But an overlap that is positive yet very small raises a separate concern about how reliably the distinction could be estimated with limited feedback. That concern does not change the hypothesis’s stated condition; it is a reason not to turn the hypothesis into a claim of easy or precise finite-feedback identification.
Does the hypothesis say each of the four conditions is sufficient by itself?

No. It presents them jointly: three repeated shared anchors, independent symmetric noise below 50%, distinct cluster signatures, and positive policy overlap. Shared anchors without distinguishable signatures would not provide the intended separation; a noise assumption without informative observations would not either. The claim to examine is whether their combination identifies persistent disagreement.
Does identifying persistent disagreement automatically identify the true group identity of each annotator?

That is not what the hypothesis states. Its conclusion is identification of persistent disagreement, separately from annotator-specific noise. It does not assert that observed group identities become available, or that every pseudonymous annotator can be assigned to a latent cluster without ambiguity. Those would be stronger claims.
Could the conditions be described as necessary?

Not on the basis of this hypothesis. It proposes that these conditions identify persistent disagreement; it does not say that no other collection of conditions could do so, or that identification is impossible whenever any one of them is absent. Calling them necessary would go beyond the stated claim.
And would it be accurate to say that the hypothesis proves three anchors are enough?

No. It hypothesizes that three repeated shared anchors are enough in combination with the other conditions. The exact number is part of what would need justification. Until an identifiability argument is established, “three are sufficient” should be presented as the proposed claim, not as a proven fact.
If I mention policy shifts, should I claim the latent clusters stay identifiable under any arbitrary shift?

No. The hypothesis includes positive policy overlap, so it is conditional on that overlap rather than a claim about arbitrary shifts. Its conclusion concerns identifying persistent disagreement when the listed conditions hold. A shift that removes the relevant overlap falls outside what the hypothesis asserts.
Is the noise assumption supposed to eliminate annotation noise from the feedback?

No. The hypothesis allows annotation noise; it constrains that noise to be independent and symmetric with a rate below 50%. The proposed conclusion is that persistent disagreement remains identifiable separately from such noise, not that every annotation is correct or that noise disappears.
Can you distinguish the proposed identifiability claim from a worst-cluster performance claim?

Yes. This hypothesis concerns whether persistent disagreement can be distinguished from annotator-specific noise under the stated anchor, signature, noise, and overlap conditions. It does not report a preference win rate, demonstrate an RLHF improvement, or establish how a worst-cluster training objective performs. Identification and performance are different claims.
What would need careful definition before presenting this as a formal statement?

At minimum, the formal statement would need to say what counts as each of the three repeated shared anchors; which observations are covered by noise independence and symmetry; how the below-50% noise rate is defined; what makes cluster signatures distinct; what comparisons positive policy overlap covers; and what, precisely, is identified. Those definitions would clarify the hypothesis without treating its conclusion as already demonstrated.
I want one faithful sentence for the hypothesis, keeping the threshold and all the conditions.

The hypothesis is that three repeated shared anchors, independent symmetric annotation noise below 50%, distinct cluster signatures, and positive policy overlap jointly identify persistent preference disagreement separately from annotator-specific noise under policy shifts.
I want to derive three-view anchor-mixture identifiability conditions, then test noise and policy-overlap boundaries in shifted-policy simulations. How should I describe the purpose of that plan?

The plan has a theoretical step followed by a simulation step. First, derive conditions under which a three-view anchor-mixture formulation can identify latent preference differences separately from annotator-specific noise. Then use shifted-policy simulations to examine the boundaries associated with noise and policy overlap. The plan addresses the question of when shared-anchor evidence remains informative under policy shifts; it does not yet state what the derived conditions or simulation results will be.
What should a reader understand by “three-view anchor-mixture” here?

It names the formulation whose identifiability conditions you plan to derive. “Anchor-mixture” indicates that anchor-based observations are being considered in relation to latent preference patterns, and “three-view” specifies the structure to be analyzed. The plan does not define exactly what constitutes each view, so it would be premature to equate the three views with a particular number of anchors, annotators, or repetitions.
Is the derivation supposed to answer whether latent preference clusters can be separated from annotator-specific noise?

Yes. That is the identifiability issue the plan addresses. The derivation should make clear under what conditions the observed anchor-based feedback distinguishes latent preference differences from annotator-specific noise, rather than merely producing a possible clustering. The plan to derive those conditions is not itself a conclusion that the separation is possible in every case.
Why do I need to call them identifiability conditions instead of just conditions for a clustering procedure to run?

Because a clustering procedure can produce assignments even when different underlying explanations yield the same observations. Identifiability asks whether the latent preference structure is distinguishable, in principle, from alternatives such as annotator-specific noise under the stated observation model. The theoretical part of the plan concerns that distinction, not just whether a procedure can output clusters.
Does “derive” mean I am promising a particular theorem already?

No. It states the intended theoretical work, not its outcome. A derivation might delimit cases where identification can be justified and cases where it cannot; the plan does not specify a theorem, proof technique, or final set of conditions in advance. Describing the work as planned keeps that uncertainty intact.
What does the word “then” commit me to?

It gives the order: derive the three-view anchor-mixture identifiability conditions first, then test noise and policy-overlap boundaries in shifted-policy simulations. It does not say the simulations have already been run, or that they will establish the theoretical conditions by themselves.
What are the simulations meant to test if the derivation is theoretical?

They are meant to examine noise and policy-overlap boundaries under shifted policies. Conceptually, that means looking at how the ability to distinguish latent preference patterns from noise behaves as those two aspects become more challenging. Simulation can probe behavior under specified scenarios, while the derivation addresses what can be identified under stated conditions. The plan does not yet say where the boundaries lie or what the simulations will show.
Should I say the simulation will prove identifiability?

No. Simulation results can illustrate or test behavior in the simulated settings, but they do not by themselves prove a general identifiability claim. Can randomized shifted-pair probes distinguish persistent minority disagreement from cluster-label drift under 45% annotator turnover?

That is an open question. Randomized probes might provide comparisons that help relate inferred preference patterns across rounds, but their randomization alone does not establish which explanation is correct. To answer it, we would need to know whether persistent minority disagreement and cluster-label drift produce distinguishable patterns in the feedback available under 45% annotator turnover.
What is the distinction between those two explanations?

Persistent minority disagreement means an underlying preference pattern continues to conflict with another pattern. Cluster-label drift concerns how inferred clusters are named or related across rounds: a pattern could appear to move between cluster labels even if the underlying disagreement persists. The question is whether probe responses let us tell a continuing preference difference from a change in the inferred labels used to represent it.
So if cluster one becomes cluster two, have preferences necessarily changed?

No. Cluster names are assigned by an inference procedure. A change in name alone does not establish a change in anyone’s preferences. It is important to compare the preference patterns associated with clusters, rather than interpret the literal labels as stable identities.
Could there also be drift more consequential than simply swapping the names?

Conceptually, yes. The inferred grouping could change in a way that makes cross-round correspondence uncertain, rather than merely swapping two names. The question does not specify a particular kind of drift, so an answer would need to define what counts as cluster-label drift before claiming that the probes distinguish it from persistent disagreement.
Why does 45% annotator turnover make this difficult?

Turnover reduces the continuity of pseudonymous annotators whose responses might otherwise help connect one round’s inferred clusters to another’s. With fewer such connections, a changed cluster description may be harder to interpret. The 45% figure specifies the annotator-turnover condition being asked about; it does not, by itself, tell us whether the distinction is possible.
Does 45% turnover mean 45% of the feedback comes from newcomers?

Not necessarily. It is a percentage of annotator turnover, not a stated percentage of labels. The question does not give the number of labels supplied by continuing or newly participating annotators, so those shares cannot be inferred from the turnover rate.
Are we assuming the annotators who remain have fixed preferences?

The question does not explicitly impose that assumption. “Persistent minority disagreement” describes the preference pattern one wants to distinguish, but an identifiability argument would need to specify what persistence means and what changes, if any, it allows across rounds. Turnover alone should not be equated with a change in the preferences of continuing annotators.
Why use randomized shifted-pair probes for this question?

They could supply feedback on comparisons relevant to the shifted setting without selecting only pairs already believed to support one inferred cluster. That may help assess whether a preference contrast remains visible as the observed distribution changes. But the question does not specify the probing distribution or guarantee that it includes pairs capable of distinguishing the competing explanations.
Would any random sample of shifted pairs suffice?

No such sufficiency follows from randomization alone. If the sampled pairs do not reveal a difference between the competing preference patterns, their responses may not distinguish persistent disagreement from drift. The probe distribution’s support and the information in the comparisons would matter; neither is specified in the question.
What does it mean for a shifted pair to be informative in this context?

At a conceptual level, an informative pair is one on which the explanations being compared have different observable implications. If both a persistent-disagreement account and a cluster-drift account predict the same responses on every probed pair, those probes cannot tell the accounts apart. This describes the inferential requirement, not a claim that particular informative pairs have been found.
If a minority-looking response appears in the new probes, does that prove the disagreement persisted?

No. An isolated response does not by itself establish a persistent preference pattern or connect it reliably to an inferred cluster from another round. A careful interpretation would ask whether a recognizable disagreement pattern remains supported by comparable observations, while accounting for uncertainty in the clusters. The question supplies no such observations yet.
How would I avoid confusing an inferred cluster with a known minority group?

Keep the descriptions separate. A cluster is an inferred grouping based on feedback; minority disagreement refers to the underlying preference difference the question is concerned with. Observing a cluster label in one round does not give us an observed annotator group identity or prove which latent preference pattern it represents after turnover.
Could responses from continuing pseudonymous annotators help connect the rounds?

In principle, responses that can be related across rounds could help assess whether an inferred preference pattern persists despite changes in cluster labels. But the question does not specify how many annotators continue, which probes they answer, or whether those responses suffice. The presence of some continuity under 45% turnover is not itself an answer.
And what if the probes only reach newcomers?

Then relating newcomer responses to earlier inferred patterns would depend on whatever shared comparisons or other observable connections are available. Without an adequate connection, different alignments of the new and earlier clusters could remain consistent with the feedback. The question does not specify who receives the probes, so neither that limitation nor its resolution should be asserted as an observed fact.
Does distinguishing the explanations require matching each newcomer to a specific earlier annotator?

Not necessarily. The substantive question is whether preference patterns can be related across rounds and separated from cluster-label drift. That is different from finding a one-to-one match between individuals. The question does not require exact assignment of every newcomer to a prior cluster, although uncertainty about assignments could affect the distinction.
If two clusters simply exchange names, is there any persistent disagreement left to identify?

There could be. An exchange of names does not eliminate the preference contrast between the underlying patterns. If comparable probe responses still distinguish those patterns, disagreement may remain visible even though the labels have switched. Whether the available randomized shifted-pair probes actually provide that comparison under 45% turnover remains open.
Could the probes distinguish the patterns but fail to tell us which one was previously called the minority cluster?

Conceptually, yes. Identifying two different preference patterns in a round is not the same as aligning each with an earlier inferred label. The question asks about separating persistent minority disagreement from label drift, so a convincing answer would need to specify which cross-round relationship is being identified, not merely show that a clustering procedure produces two labels.
Do the probes establish a cause for any drift they reveal?

No. Even if a test found that cluster labels changed, probe observations alone would not automatically establish why the inferred labels changed. The question concerns whether the competing interpretations can be distinguished, not a demonstrated causal account of drift.
Could annotation variability make this distinction harder too?

Yes, as a general inferential consideration: variable annotations could obscure the response patterns used to relate clusters across rounds. But the question specifies no noise rate or model. We should not introduce one as an established condition or claim that the randomized probes already separate noise from persistent disagreement.
What would a negative answer mean?

It would mean that, under the specified observations and assumptions of an actual assessment, persistent minority disagreement and cluster-label drift cannot be reliably separated by those probes. It would not automatically mean minority preferences have disappeared, that turnover changes preferences, or that no other observations could help. No negative answer has been established here.
And what would a positive answer need to demonstrate?

It would need to show that the randomized shifted-pair responses contain enough information to relate preference patterns across rounds despite 45% turnover, so that a continuing minority preference contrast cannot be explained equally well as cluster-label drift under the assumptions being used. It would also need to keep inferred labels distinct from observed group identities. The present question does not provide that demonstration.

Under 45% annotator turnover, do randomized shifted-pair probes provide enough cross-round evidence to distinguish persistent minority preference disagreement from drift in inferred cluster labels?

Since the broader question mentions randomized shifted-pair probes, should I say these three repeated probes are already randomized?

What does it mean to align clusters here?

Full rank is the proposed condition that the anchor structure carries enough independent information for the cluster distinctions being aligned. Does full rank mean we have observed every possible annotator group?

No. Rank describes an information property of the anchors under an eventual formal definition; it does not supply observed group identities. Even informative anchors would not, by themselves, establish that every underlying preference group has been found.
Is 10% minority shifted-pair coverage just another way of saying 10% overall policy overlap?

No. The condition concerns minority shifted-pair coverage, not an aggregate overlap measure. Comparisons may overlap overall without covering the shifted pairs pertinent to minority preference differences. Those quantities should not be substituted for one another.
Can I call the 10% a fraction of newcomers whose clusters are aligned?

No. It is a coverage percentage for minority shifted pairs, not an alignment rate or a percentage of newcomers. The proposed conclusion—cluster alignment—has no numerical success rate stated in this hypothesis.
How can I state a minority-specific coverage condition if group identities are unobserved?

Am I claiming that three probes work under every possible turnover rate?

Is the hypothesis saying these conditions are necessary for alignment?

No. It is phrased as a conditional prediction: if the specified coverage and anchor conditions hold despite 45% turnover, three repeated probes per newcomer align clusters. It does not say alignment is impossible without three probes, without that coverage level, or without those anchors.
Does it guarantee alignment merely because all the conditions appear in the sentence?

It hypothesizes alignment when they hold; it does not establish that outcome. The probe scheme and conditions would need a defined model and supporting argument or test before the conditional claim could be treated as demonstrated.

Does it separate persistent preferences from annotator-specific noise as well?

If minority shifted-pair coverage is 10% but the anchors are not full rank, does the hypothesis predict alignment?

No prediction for that case follows from this conditional statement. Both 10% minority shifted-pair coverage and full-rank anchors are specified as conditions. If either does not hold, the hypothesis does not say whether the probes succeed or fail.

That also falls outside the stated conditions. The hypothesis does not establish an impossibility below 10%; it simply does not make its alignment prediction for that case.

No. Cluster alignment is an inference outcome. A worst-group preference win-rate improvement would require a trained-policy performance comparison. This hypothesis reports no win rates, comparator, or feedback-budget comparison.

I’d like to propose DecorrAnchor-RLHF: randomize anchor paraphrases across independent annotator panels, test for shared prompt artifacts, and only then proceed to coverage-gated minimax training. Can you unpack it as a proposal rather than a result?

DecorrAnchor-RLHF proposes an order of operations. First, it randomizes paraphrases of anchor comparisons across independent annotator panels. It then tests whether apparent agreement or disagreement may reflect shared prompt artifacts. Coverage-gated minimax training comes afterward. The proposal does not report the outcome of the artifact test, establish that the panels’ annotations are statistically independent, or demonstrate a worst-group performance gain.
What are “anchor paraphrases” doing in this proposal?

They provide differently worded versions of anchor comparisons for examining whether the wording itself affects the feedback used to infer preferences. Calling them paraphrases expresses an intended relationship between the versions; it does not establish that every version is perfectly equivalent or that a particular paraphrase set has already been validated.
Why randomize them rather than present one version to everyone?

Randomization is the proposed way to avoid tying an observed response pattern exclusively to one chosen wording and panel assignment. It may help examine whether the pattern persists across paraphrases. But randomization alone does not prove the absence of prompt artifacts or establish that differences in responses represent persistent preference disagreement.
Does the proposal specify a randomization scheme?

No. It says to randomize anchor paraphrases across independent annotator panels, without specifying the probabilities, the number of paraphrases, or how any version is assigned. Those would be additional implementation details.
What makes the panels independent? Does that mean their annotation noise is independent?

The proposal calls them independent annotator panels, but it does not formally define panel independence or state a noise model. Separate panels should not automatically be treated as proof that their annotation errors are independent. Testing for a shared prompt artifact is still meaningful precisely because a feature of the presented comparison could affect feedback across panels.
Can I describe these as panels with known annotator group identities?

No. Independent annotator panels are not the same thing as observed annotator preference groups. The proposal does not grant group labels, and distributing paraphrases across panels does not reveal the underlying preference-group identities of their members.
Could each panel simply stand for a different minority preference component?

That would add an assumption the proposal does not make. A panel describes a collection of annotators used for the proposed comparison; a latent preference component describes a pattern one might try to infer. Nothing here establishes a one-to-one correspondence between panels and components.
What counts as a shared prompt artifact conceptually?

It is a response pattern attributable to something shared in how the prompt or comparison is presented, rather than necessarily to a persistent difference in the preferences being studied. The proposal calls for testing that possibility. It does not identify a particular artifact, say one has been found, or prescribe a definitive test for every possible prompt effect.
If two panels agree on an anchor, does that rule out a shared artifact?

No. An artifact shared by the presentation could influence more than one panel. Agreement alone would not establish why annotators responded alike. The proposed paraphrase randomization and artifact test are intended to examine that interpretive ambiguity, not to make agreement self-validating.
What if panels disagree? Is that automatically evidence of a conflicting minority preference?

No. Disagreement could have more than one explanation, including a difference in preferences, annotation variability, or a response to how paraphrases are worded. DecorrAnchor-RLHF proposes to test for shared prompt artifacts before treating anchor-based patterns as suitable input to its subsequent training step. It does not say every remaining disagreement has been identified as a persistent minority preference.
Does varying paraphrases risk changing the actual comparison being judged?

That is an important interpretive concern. If paraphrases differ in a way relevant to the choice, different responses need not be artifacts of an otherwise equivalent prompt. The proposal does not define how semantic equivalence is established, so a description should not assume that all paraphrases preserve precisely the same comparison.
Is the purpose to remove all annotation noise?

No. The specified test concerns shared prompt artifacts. A test for prompt-related effects is not, by itself, a method for eliminating every form of annotation noise or identifying every persistent preference difference. The proposal leaves those broader inferential questions open.
How are shared prompt artifacts different from annotator-specific noise?

They refer to different potential sources of response variation. A shared prompt artifact is associated with how a comparison is presented and could affect multiple annotators; annotator-specific noise concerns variation attributed to individual annotations or annotators. The proposal calls for a test of the former, without supplying a model that fully separates it from the latter.
And how is an artifact different from cluster-label drift?

An artifact concerns the presented prompt; cluster-label drift concerns whether inferred cluster labels continue to represent corresponding preference patterns across observations. A prompt effect could complicate cluster inference, but testing for it is not automatically a complete test for label drift. The proposal does not claim to settle both issues.
What does “before coverage-gated minimax training” require?

It makes the paraphrase randomization and shared-prompt-artifact test precede the coverage-gated minimax training stage. It does not say the training has already happened, specify the test’s pass rule, or guarantee that the eventual training stage will improve a worst-group win rate.
Is the prompt-artifact test itself the coverage gate?

Not as stated. The proposal names a test for shared prompt artifacts before coverage-gated minimax training. A prompt-artifact check concerns how to interpret responses; a coverage gate concerns whether the relevant comparison feedback is sufficiently represented. The proposal does not equate those checks or give a numerical coverage threshold.
Could I say that passing the artifact test automatically satisfies the coverage gate?

No. Evidence against a shared prompt artifact would not, on its own, show that minority-relevant shifted comparisons are covered. The two questions concern different limitations. This proposal does not specify how either check is implemented or establish that one implies the other.
Does “minimax” here tell us the exact training objective?

It identifies the subsequent training approach as coverage-gated minimax training, with attention to a poorly served preference outcome rather than just an undifferentiated pooled average. The proposal does not specify an objective formula, how latent components are inferred, or how the worst component is selected.
Should I say DecorrAnchor-RLHF guarantees correct minority clusters once the artifact test is done?

No. Testing for shared prompt artifacts could inform how anchor responses are interpreted, but it does not automatically establish correct cluster assignments or prove that persistent minority disagreement is identifiable separately from noise. Neither a successful test nor a cluster-recovery result is reported.
What if the artifact test suggests a prompt effect? Does the proposal say what happens next?

It does not specify a response or a decision rule for that outcome. It says to test before coverage-gated minimax training, but gives no prescribed way to change the anchors, repeat the test, or handle an inconclusive result. Those should remain open rather than being described as decisions already made.
Would it be accurate to call this a proven solution to correlated noise?

No. It proposes randomizing anchor paraphrases across independent panels and testing for shared prompt artifacts. That is not a demonstrated remedy for every kind of correlated noise, and the proposal supplies no test result showing that correlations have been eliminated.
Does the proposal specify how many panels or labels it uses?
No. It provides no panel count, paraphrase count, label budget, or allocation between the testing and training stages. Adding numerical design details would go beyond the proposal.
Could I nonetheless claim a matched-feedback improvement over pooled RLHF?

Not from this proposal. It reports neither feedback accounting nor worst-group win rates for DecorrAnchor-RLHF and pooled RLHF. The costs of collecting paraphrase feedback would have to be accounted for in any future matched-budget comparison, but no such comparison is established here.
What is the main inferential caution behind the design?

A pattern on shared anchors should not automatically be treated as persistent disagreement between latent preference components if the prompts themselves might create a shared response pattern. DecorrAnchor-RLHF proposes using randomized paraphrases across independent panels to examine that possibility before coverage-gated minimax training. Whether that examination can reliably distinguish the explanations remains an open question.
Can I describe the approach without implying that paraphrase variation is always harmless?

Yes. Say the paraphrases are randomized *to test* for shared prompt artifacts, not that they are guaranteed equivalent or that randomizing them removes all effects of wording. Their interpretation is part of what the proposed test would need to support.
Does an observed worst-group gain, if one is later measured, prove the artifact test was correct?

No. Policy performance and the validity of a prompt-artifact test are separate claims. A later gain would need its own evaluation, and it would not automatically establish why the anchor feedback had the patterns it did. This proposal provides neither finding.
Can you give me a concise sentence with the method name and the intended order?
DecorrAnchor-RLHF proposes randomizing anchor paraphrases across independent annotator panels, testing for shared prompt artifacts, and then proceeding to coverage-gated minimax training.
Can independent-panel anchor paraphrases identify shared prompt artifacts without mistaking persistent minority preferences for correlated noise?

That is an open identifiability question. Paraphrases presented across independent annotator panels could help examine whether a response pattern follows the wording of an anchor or reflects a preference disagreement that persists across presentations. But independent panels and varied wording do not, by themselves, establish which explanation is correct. An answer would need conditions under which a shared prompt artifact, correlated noise, and persistent minority preferences have distinguishable implications for the observed responses.
What exactly would count as a shared prompt artifact here?

Conceptually, it would be a response pattern associated with something shared in how an anchor comparison is presented, rather than with the underlying preference distinction the anchor is intended to reveal. The question does not specify a particular artifact or a rule for declaring that one has been identified. It asks whether using paraphrases across panels can help make that distinction.
How is that different from correlated noise?

A shared prompt artifact concerns a feature of the presented comparison that may influence responses across annotators. Correlated noise concerns annotation variability that is not independent across relevant observations. The two might look similar in feedback, but they are not definitions of each other. Finding a pattern shared across panels would not automatically tell us whether it arose from presentation, correlated annotation variability, or a persistent preference.
And persistent minority preferences could also produce a recurring pattern?

Yes. That is the central caution in the question: a recurring difference need not be noise or an artifact merely because it appears among a subset of responses. If people with a persistent minority preference consistently favor a different outcome, treating that pattern as correlated noise would erase the very disagreement one wants to recognize. The question asks how to avoid that mistake while still identifying prompt effects.
Do independent annotator panels guarantee independent annotation errors?

No. Independence of panels describes how the annotator panels are organized; it does not, without further assumptions, prove statistical independence of their errors or eliminate an influence shared by the prompts they see. The question relies on comparing information across panels, not on assuming that any common pattern must be a true preference—or must be an artifact.
Could I interpret each panel as a known preference group?

No. A panel is an observation setting, not an observed annotator preference group. The panels may contain people with different latent preferences, and the question does not grant knowledge of their group identities. Equating panel membership with minority-preference membership would make the inference seem resolved before examining the responses.
What are the paraphrases supposed to help distinguish?

They offer differently worded presentations of an anchor comparison. In principle, variation across presentations could make a wording-linked response pattern observable, while a preference contrast that remains recognizable across suitably comparable presentations might support a different interpretation. That distinction depends on what the paraphrases preserve, how they are assigned across panels, and which response patterns are compared. None of those conditions has been established by the question alone.
If responses differ across paraphrases, have we identified an artifact?

Not automatically. The paraphrases might differ in a way that changes what is being judged, or the responding panels might differ in their latent preferences. A difference in responses is evidence to interpret, not a self-evident diagnosis. Identifying a shared prompt artifact would require a defensible distinction between a presentation effect and a genuine preference response to a meaningfully different comparison.
So do we need the paraphrases to mean exactly the same thing?

The interpretation would need an account of which aspects of the anchor comparison the paraphrases are meant to preserve. Calling them paraphrases does not prove perfect equivalence. If a change in wording changes a preference-relevant feature, different judgments may be genuine responses to different comparisons rather than noise or a spurious artifact. The question does not specify an equivalence criterion.
What if the same minority-looking judgment appears under every paraphrase?

That could be consistent with persistent minority disagreement, but it would not establish it on its own. A shared feature retained by every paraphrase could also influence responses, and other dependencies could remain. The question calls for conditions that make those explanations separable, rather than treating consistency across paraphrases as a conclusive test.
What if only one panel produces the minority-looking judgment?

That also has multiple possible interpretations. It might reflect a preference pattern present among that panel’s participants, an effect of which paraphrase they received, or variation in annotations. Without enough information to separate panel composition from presentation and noise, calling it either a genuine minority preference or correlated noise would be premature.
Would randomizing paraphrases across panels address that ambiguity?

Randomization could help keep paraphrase choice from being systematically tied to panel assignment, depending on how it is carried out. But it cannot by itself reveal unobserved preference-group membership or guarantee that all relevant preference patterns are represented. The question is whether independent-panel paraphrases provide enough information to separate the explanations, not whether the word “randomized” settles them.
Does a pattern repeated across independent panels necessarily count as persistent disagreement?

No. Repetition across panels may be informative, but something shared in the presentation could affect both panels. Conversely, a real minority preference might appear at different frequencies across panels. The substantive issue is whether the pattern tracks a stable preference contrast rather than merely tracking a prompt feature or correlated annotation variability.
Would it be safer just to label any disagreement as noise until proven otherwise?

That would prejudge the distinction the question is trying to make. Persistent minority preferences are a possible source of disagreement, not a residual category to discard automatically. Equally, treating every conflicting response as a distinct persistent preference would ignore artifacts and noise. The purpose of the proposed comparison across paraphrases and panels is to investigate those possibilities without assuming one in advance.
Can a shared prompt artifact coexist with a genuine minority preference?

Conceptually, yes. The possibility of a prompt effect does not logically rule out an underlying preference difference, and a preference difference does not guarantee prompts have no effect. An answer would need to consider whether the available observations can distinguish their contributions, rather than forcing every response pattern into exactly one explanation. The question does not supply a model for doing that.
Would a test that flags correlated responses be enough to protect minority preferences?

Not without interpreting what is correlated. Responses reflecting a stable, conflicting preference could also exhibit a recognizable common pattern. A flag for dependence alone does not show that the pattern is annotation noise, nor that it is a shared prompt artifact. Avoiding the mistake named in the question requires a way to distinguish dependence due to persistent preference differences from dependence attributed to noise or presentation.
Does the question ask us to eliminate prompt artifacts?

It asks whether independent-panel anchor paraphrases can *identify* shared prompt artifacts without misclassifying persistent minority preferences as correlated noise. Identifying a possible artifact, removing its effects, and improving a trained policy are separate claims. No removal procedure or outcome is specified here.
How would I frame a useful positive answer without overclaiming?

It would need to specify assumptions and observable patterns under which paraphrase- and panel-linked effects can be distinguished from stable minority preference disagreement, including how correlated noise is treated. Then it could say what the evidence establishes under those assumptions and what remains ambiguous. The present question offers neither those conditions nor a positive finding.
What would make a negative or inconclusive answer possible?

If a shared prompt effect and a persistent minority preference could generate the same observable responses across the available paraphrases and panels, those observations would not separate them. Likewise, if correlated noise were allowed to mimic the persistent pattern without an observable difference, a confident classification would be unwarranted. Those are conceptual limits to examine, not reported findings about a particular evaluation.
Does comparing panels require following the same annotator across them?

The question does not require or specify that the same person belongs to multiple panels. Independent-panel evidence could be compared at the level of responses to anchor paraphrases, but connecting those responses to latent preferences remains an inferential task. It would be incorrect to assume either cross-panel identity tracking or observed preference-group labels merely from the panel design.
Could we use the literal name of an inferred cluster to recognize a persistent minority preference across panels?

Not by itself. Cluster labels are assigned names; the same name need not denote the same preference pattern in different panels, and different names need not denote different patterns. The question concerns whether anchor-paraphrase responses reveal a substantive, persistent preference distinction, not whether cluster names match.
Do policy-induced distribution shifts still matter to this question?

They matter to the broader interpretation of anchor feedback: when the comparisons observed under a policy change, an apparent difference can reflect what was presented as well as how it was annotated. But this question does not specify particular shifts, support-overlap levels, or a shifted-policy result. We should not attach numerical shift conditions or claim that the paraphrase design already handles every shift.
Does answering this question also establish that worst-group RLHF performance improves?

No. Distinguishing prompt artifacts and correlated noise from persistent minority preferences is an inference question. Worst-group win rate is a policy-performance measure. Even a convincing answer about the anchor feedback would not, without a separate evaluation, establish a win-rate gain over pooled RLHF.

Can anchor paraphrases compared across independent annotator panels reveal shared prompt artifacts while preserving the distinction between correlated annotation noise and genuine, persistent minority preference disagreement?

It proposes a diagnostic contrast across independent annotator panels and anchor paraphrases. The intended contrast is that the preference patterns remain relatively stable while residual agreement changes substantially in relation to the paraphrase comparison. “Invariance” should not be read as saying every measured quantity stays unchanged. What does residual agreement mean in that sentence?

It names the agreement quantity being compared after some other structure has been accounted for. Is the 15-point condition a change in average preference win rate?

What is supposed to remain within 5 points?

The stable cluster preferences. That condition is distinct from the ≥15-point shift in residual agreement.
